blocks.text: Hamiltons Gallery exhibits a new selection of exceptional works by Charles Jones , previously unseen. In 1998 Hamiltons Gallery presented the first ever exhibition of photographs by Charles Jones, coinciding with the publication of The Plant Kingdom of Charles Jones by Thames & Hudson. In the nearly thirty years since, the works have been widely exhibited, including at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, the Musée de l’Elysée in Lausanne, the Dulwich Picture Gallery in London and the Konstmuseet Gothenburg.

Little is known about the life of Charles Jones, aside from the fact he was born in Wolverhampton in 1866 and was employed as a professional gardener at many notable private estates across England. Even less was known about his photographic oeuvre until it was rediscovered by historian and photographic collector Sean Sexton. In 1981, two decades after Jones’ death, Sexton found a trove of signed gold-toned gelatin silver prints in a trunk offered for sale at Bermondsey Antiques Market. The works are estimated to have been produced between 1895 and 1910.

Working from glass-plate negatives, Jones was an exceptionally skilled printer and had a meticulous approach to composition and tone. Most of his photographs isolate their subjects against neutral dark or light backgrounds. Captured at close range with long exposures, the specimens appear highly detailed, their forms rendered with delicate contrast and minimal shadow. His works both belong to a long tradition of depicting the natural world as well as anticipate that which would preoccupy modernist artists such as Edward Weston and Alfred Stieglitz. No known negatives belonging to Jones exist.

Jones photographed the flowers, fruits and vegetables that he grew on the grounds of Great Ote Hall in Sussex where he held the position of Head Gardener from 1893 to 1905. A 1905 article in Gardener’s Chronicle noted Jones’ work at Great Ote Hall: “Mr Jones is quite an enthusiastic fruit grower and his delight in his well-trained trees was readily apparent…. The appearance of crops denoted the all-round capability of the man in charge; and that it does not stop at gardening is testified by the many excellent views from photographs taken by his camera which appear from time to time in the gardening press.”

The images possess a distinct sensuality. From beans – open and closed – to cabbages and turnips, Jones documents vegetables as fecund and engorged. The antecedent for this stretches a great distance back into art history, seen in the sumptuous fruits of Raphael’s frescoes in the Loggia di Psyche at the Villa Farnesina in Rome to Dutch still life paintings of the seventeenth century.

Jones’ work represents not only an innate artistic sensibility but a gardener’s scientific rigor. The images often contain annotations in Jones’ script, creating a dialectical relationship between artist and gardener. Horticultural photography was an expensive hobby in the late Victorian era and the reverence of Jones’ images bestows a quiet dignity on his subject matter.

The bucolic rural England that Jones inhabited was rapidly changing around the time he was taking these photographs. The second industrial revolution was unfolding, leading to mass production and fast-moving scientific discoveries such as electrical lightbulbs and expanding railways. Massive urbanisation saw the creation of metropolitan city centres as the British Empire reached the height of its global dominance. The photographs of Charles Jones are extraordinary objects and all the more remarkable for having been created at the turn of the twentieth century.
Charles Jones Unseen 25 November 2026 – 30 January 2027 Hamiltons Gallery 13 Carlos Place London W1K 2EU +44 (0) 207 499 9493 www.hamiltonsgallery.com
